extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and applicants/litigants involved in appeals and interference proceedings before the Commissioner and the District Court
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing appeals from the Commissioner of Patents (acts of 1836/1839), the scope of review by the District Court Chief Justice, and substantive criteria for priority, inventorship, interference, and patentability (including combinations vs elemental devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of time and abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is no limitation unless the lapse of time be sufficient to show an abandonment of the invention, which is a question for the jury and not for the Commissioner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay between invention and application does not automatically bar a claim; only when lapse indicates abandonment (a factual question for a jury) may delay defeat rights. Commissioner should not treat mere lapse as conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of application does not equal priority of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nor does the priority of application for a patent decide the priority of invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing date/priority of application is not dispositive of who first invented; separate factual inquiry on who first invented may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower evidentiary standard in Commissioner proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: “The proceedings before the Commissioner of Patents are initiatory. The question is, ‘whether the patent shall be granted,’ not ‘whether it shall be vacated;’ and a patent may be granted or refused upon less evidence than would be required to sustain or amend it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions on initial grant/ refusal by the Commissioner can be made on a lower quantum/quality of proof than would be needed to sustain or overturn an already-granted patent in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of the constructor/creator absent contrary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where evidence shows Boardman constructed the pump and improvements, “the presumption, therefore, is that he was also the inventor, and the burden of proof is thrown upon Mr. Atkinson to show, not merely that he first suggested the abstract idea... but that he invented the improvements which entitle it to a patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant actually built and directed construction of an invention, courts will presume inventorship unless the challenger produces affirmative evidence showing another person invented the patentable improvements (mere suggestion is insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and limited weight of unilateral declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have not considered the declarations of the parties in their own favor, in the absence of each other, as competent evidence in this cause for any purpose but to ascertain when and what they have respectively claimed to have invented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-serving statements made in the absence of the other party are of limited evidentiary value — useful primarily to show what each party later claimed, not to establish inventorship on their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of employment/agency evidence to inventorship/ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: The court notes lack of evidence that Boardman “was in the employment and pay of Mr. Atkinson” and treats employment/agency evidence as relevant to claims of ownership/inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that an alleged inventor was employed/paid by another at the time of invention can affect entitlement and assignment issues; absence or presence of such evidence is material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of probative evidence for inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion cites models, drawings, who paid for construction, orders, witness testimony about who drafted, directed, or exhibited the device (e.g., patterns, sketches, payments, construction for underwriters) as evidence of who invented or created the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes, look for contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence — models, drawings, payment records, orders, witness recollections of construction/exhibition — to prove inventorship or priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal jurisdiction limited to specified decisions under statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where the decision of the Commissioner... neither affirms or denies the right of the applicant to the patent (which he claims) upon the merits... it is not such a decision as is the subject of appeal under the act of July 4, 1836, ... and ... the act of March 3, 1839... and that therefore I have not jurisdiction of this appeal, which is therefore hereby dismissed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeal to the District Court exists only for the types of Commissioner decisions specified by the 1836/1839 acts (e.g., refusal to grant a patent after examination). If the Commissioner merely refuses to reopen or reconsider a prior examiner decision without ruling on the merits, the judge may lack jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge’s scope of review includes interference and priority where appealed
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge may decide whether a real interference exists and, in such case, “determine which, or whether either of the applicants is entitled to receive a patent as prayed for.” The judge’s revision is “confined” to the points involved by the reasons of appeal, but that includes interference when raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interference (priority dispute) is raised in the reasons of appeal, the District Court may examine interference and priority questions and determine entitlement to a patent, subject to the statutory confinement to issues pleaded in the appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner’s opinion is not conclusive; board/judge may reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 (1836) contemplates that when the Commissioner considers a specification/claim not allowable, he may order a board of examiners whose opinion may reverse the Commissioner: the legislature did not intend the Commissioner’s opinion to be conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative decisions include procedures for internal review (board of examiners) and external appeal; the Commissioner’s written grounds must be furnished and can be revisited by the board or judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference must concern patentable matter and claims are limited to their specification
rubrics_metrics.description: “The interference mentioned... must be an interference in respect to patentable matters; and the claims of the applicants must be limited to the matters specifically set forth, as their respective inventions; and what is not thus claimed, may, for the purpose of this preliminary inquiry, be considered as disclaimed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only overlaps in patentable subject-matter as specifically claimed trigger interference; unclaimed subject-matter should be treated as disclaimed for interference analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether an interference exists: compare claimed patentable matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “The question then is, does Mr. Bain claim a patent for any matter now patentable, for which Mr. Morse claims a patent? To answer this question, it is necessary to ascertain for what patentable matter Mr. Morse now claims a patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine interference by construing each party’s claims/specifications to see if they claim the same patentable subject-matter; focus on what each party actually claims as their invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of combinations vs elemental features
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner found that elemental features (single circuit, prepared paper, marking by electro-chemical process) were not new, so they were not patentable alone; but a novel combination of known elements producing a new or better result can be patentable: “it was only a new combination of the several parts so as to produce a new result, or an old result in a better manner, that either could patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim monopoly over long-known elementary devices or natural forces alone; instead, claim a novel combination or application that yields a new/result or improved operation. Assess novelty and patentability at the combination level when elements are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be read in light of specification (claim construction rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court analyzed Morse’s claim language (use of a single circuit to mark telegraphic signs and the machinery described) to determine the scope and whether Bain’s claims interfered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is central: read claims per specification to identify scope, elemental features, and whether the competing claim falls within that scope for interference and patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory time bar for appeal in certain circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no limitation of time as to the appeal; and I do not perceive any reason why Mr. Janney may not now appeal from the decision of Mr. Ellsworth, and have the merits of his invention decided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some contexts described, appeals are not subject to a fixed statutory time bar; practitioners should check the applicable statutory provisions and facts, but the court recognized that some appeals may be taken later to obtain merits review.
